facts: Biggin Hill was one of the most important RAF fighter stations during the Battle of Britain.
The airport today handles private and business aviation, alongside a small museum on its wartime history.
It sits on high ground in the North Downs, giving it its wartime nickname 'Biggin on the Bump'.
The British Museum holds over 8 million objects spanning two million years of human history.
It was the first national public museum in the world, opening in 1759.
The Rosetta Stone, key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, has been on display there since 1802.
Covent Garden was London's main fruit and vegetable market for over 300 years before moving out in 1974.
The area's central piazza was designed in the 1630s by architect Inigo Jones.
It is now known for street performers, boutique shops and the Royal Opera House.
Hyde Park covers 350 acres, one of the largest of London's Royal Parks.
Speakers' Corner, at its northeast edge, has hosted public debate and oratory since the 1870s.
The Serpentine lake within the park was created in the 1730s for Queen Caroline.
Piccadilly Circus has been a major road junction since 1819.
Its illuminated advertising signs have been a landmark since the early 20th century.
The Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain at its centre is popularly known as Eros, though the statue actually depicts Anteros.
Rainham Marshes is one of the last remaining wild grazing marshes on the Thames, managed by the RSPB.
The site was formerly used as a military firing range before conservation work began.
It is an important habitat for water voles and wintering wildfowl.
Somerset House was built in the 1770s on the site of an earlier Tudor palace.
It now hosts art exhibitions, a famous winter ice rink, and summer fountains in its courtyard.
The building originally housed government offices including the Navy Board.
St Paul's Cathedral was designed by Sir Christopher Wren after the Great Fire of London destroyed its medieval predecessor.
Its dome remains one of the most recognisable features of the London skyline.
Winston Churchill's funeral was held there in 1965.
The Thames Barrier protects London from tidal surges, operational since 1982.
It consists of ten steel gates that can be raised to hold back the tide.
The barrier has been closed more frequently in recent decades as sea levels have risen.
The Shard is the tallest building in the United Kingdom, standing 310 metres tall.
It was designed by architect Renzo Piano, inspired by London's church spires and ships' masts.
Its viewing platform offers views stretching up to 40 miles on a clear day.
Trafalgar Square commemorates Admiral Nelson's victory at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805.
Nelson's Column at its centre stands over 50 metres tall including the statue.
The square's fourth plinth has hosted a rotating programme of contemporary art since 1999.
Waterloo is the largest railway station in the UK by floor area.
It was named after the Battle of Waterloo, fought in 1815.
The station was extensively rebuilt in the early 20th century, with its grand Victory Arch added after the First World War.
Westminster Abbey has hosted every English and British coronation since 1066.
It is the resting place of numerous monarchs, scientists, poets and statesmen.
The Abbey is a UNESCO World Heritage Site alongside the neighbouring Houses of Parliament.
The Royal Observatory marks the Prime Meridian, the line of zero degrees longitude.
It was founded in 1675 by Charles II to improve navigation at sea.
Greenwich Mean Time takes its name from the observatory's role in setting the world's standard time.
The Cutty Sark is one of the last surviving tea clippers, built in 1869.
It once held the record for the fastest passage from China to Britain carrying tea.
The ship is preserved in dry dock at Greenwich, raised above the ground on display.
Eltham Palace combines a medieval royal palace with a striking 1930s Art Deco mansion built alongside it.
Henry VIII spent much of his childhood at the medieval palace.
The site is now managed by English Heritage.
Chislehurst Caves are man-made chalk and flint mines dating back around 8,000 years in parts.
They were used as a deep air raid shelter for thousands of people during the Blitz.
The caves have also hosted concerts, including early performances by David Bowie and Led Zeppelin.
Charlton House is considered one of the finest surviving Jacobean houses in London, completed in 1612.
It was built for Adam Newton, tutor to Prince Henry, son of James I.
The house now serves as a community centre and library.
The Royal Arsenal at Woolwich manufactured munitions and artillery for over 200 years.
Arsenal Football Club began here in 1886 as a team of arsenal workers.
The former Arsenal site has been redeveloped into riverside housing and heritage buildings.
William Blake reported having a childhood vision of angels in a tree on Peckham Rye Common.
Peckham has become known for its vibrant street art and creative community.
The area's rooftop car park has been transformed into a popular bar and events venue.
Brixton Market has been a hub of Caribbean culture and trade in London since the mid-20th century.
The area became a centre of the Windrush generation's community in Britain.
Brixton's covered arcades host a mix of traditional stalls and newer independent food outlets.
The area's unusual name is thought to derive from a former coaching inn sign.
Elephant & Castle has undergone major redevelopment in the 2010s and 2020s.
It sits at a key road and rail junction in south London.
Blackheath has hosted major public gatherings for centuries, including Wat Tyler's 1381 Peasants' Revolt camp.
The London Marathon has started from Blackheath every year since 1981.
The heath sits between Greenwich Park and the historic village of Blackheath.
Smithfield has been a meat market site for over 800 years.
Farringdon is a major Elizabeth Line and Thameslink interchange.
The area sits at the boundary of the City of London and Clerkenwell.
The British Library holds over 170 million items, one of the largest collections in the world.
St Pancras International is the London terminus for Eurostar services to mainland Europe.
The station's Victorian train shed roof was, for a time, the largest single-span structure in the world.
Lewisham is a major south London transport and shopping hub.
The area developed rapidly after the arrival of the railway in the 1850s.
Lewisham sits on the River Ravensbourne.
Kidbrooke has seen one of London's largest housing regeneration projects, replacing a 1960s estate.
The area sits close to the Royal Blackheath Golf Club, one of the oldest golf clubs in England.
Kidbrooke station was rebuilt as part of the area's redevelopment.
Petts Wood is an area of ancient woodland managed by the National Trust.
The suburb takes its name from a family of shipbuilders who once owned timber rights here.
A war memorial in the woods commemorates William Willett, the campaigner behind British Summer Time.
Orpington Priory dates from the 14th century and now houses a local museum.
The town gave its name to the Orpington breed of chicken, developed there in the 1880s.
Orpington is one of the busiest stations on Southeastern's outer suburban network.
Danson Park is built around Danson House, a Palladian villa completed in 1766.
The park includes a large lake used for boating.
Bexleyheath developed rapidly as a London suburb following the railway's arrival.
Red House was designed for William Morris in 1859, a key building in the Arts and Crafts movement.
Morris and his collaborators decorated much of the house's interior themselves.
It is now cared for by the National Trust.
Hall Place is a mix of 16th-century Tudor and 17th-century additions, set in formal gardens.
Its topiary garden includes animal shapes representing the Queen's Beasts.
The house overlooks the River Cray.
Crayford was historically a centre of vehicle and armaments manufacturing.
The town sits on the River Cray in the London Borough of Bexley.
Crayford developed rapidly as an industrial suburb in the early 20th century.
Erith sits on the south bank of the Thames, historically an industrial and shipbuilding area.
The town has undergone significant riverside redevelopment in recent years.
Erith Pier offers views across the Thames towards Essex.
Falconwood sits close to Eltham Park, a large area of public green space.
The station serves a mainly residential area on the southeastern edge of London.
Falconwood is on the North Kent Line towards Dartford.
Lesnes Abbey was founded in 1178, its ruins now sitting within a public park.
Abbey Wood became a major Elizabeth Line terminus station in 2022.
The surrounding woodland is known for its wild daffodils each spring.
Plumstead Common was saved from enclosure by 19th-century public protests.
The area sits close to the former Royal Arsenal at Woolwich.
Plumstead developed rapidly as a working-class suburb linked to the Arsenal's workforce.
New Cross is home to a campus of Goldsmiths, University of London.
The area has a strong association with music venues and student culture.
New Cross sits at a historic road junction on the old Dover road.
Deptford was home to a major royal dockyard from the time of Henry VIII until 1869.
Christopher Marlowe, the Elizabethan playwright, was killed in a tavern brawl in Deptford in 1593.
The area has become known for its street market and creative community.
Herne Hill Velodrome hosted cycling events at the 1948 London Olympics.
It is the oldest cycling track still in use in the world.
The area developed as a leafy Victorian suburb of south London.
King's College Hospital is one of London's largest teaching hospitals.
Denmark Hill takes its name from Prince George of Denmark, husband of Queen Anne.
The area sits between Camberwell and Herne Hill.
Dulwich Picture Gallery, opened in 1817, was the first purpose-built public art gallery in England.
It was designed by architect Sir John Soane.
The gallery holds an important collection of Old Master paintings.
Crystal Palace Park was created to house the relocated Great Exhibition building from Hyde Park.
The park still contains Victorian-era dinosaur sculptures.
The Crystal Palace itself burned down in 1936.
Beckenham Place Park is one of the largest parks in south London, covering over 200 acres.
It was once the grounds of an 18th-century mansion, now used as a cafe and events space.
The park includes a large area of ancient woodland.
Grove Park developed as a residential suburb following the arrival of the railway in the 1870s.
The area sits between Lee and Chislehurst in southeast London.
Grove Park station is a key junction on the line towards Bromley and Orpington.
Author H.G. Wells was born in Bromley in 1866.
Bromley is the largest town centre in southeast London.
Bromley South is one of the busiest stations on the Southeastern network.
Sidcup developed rapidly as a residential suburb in the interwar years.
The area sits within the London Borough of Bexley.
Sidcup station is on the line towards Dartford via Sidcup.
Swanley developed around fruit growing and market gardening in the 19th century.
The town sits on the border of Greater London and Kent.
Swanley was one of the stations added to London's fare zone 8 in 2016.
Elmstead Woods station takes its name from the surrounding ancient woodland.
The area sits between Chislehurst and Grove Park.
It is a quiet residential suburb in the London Borough of Bromley.
Nunhead Cemetery is one of London's 'Magnificent Seven' Victorian cemeteries, opened in 1840.
It is now managed partly as a nature reserve, with dense woodland reclaiming many older graves.
The cemetery chapel offers views across to St Paul's Cathedral from its highest point.
